strengths: Well-motivated practical problem addressing a real bottleneck in NeRF dataset creation for 3D generative models
Strong empirical results with 86% training time reduction and 68% memory reduction per scene in stage 2, demonstrated across multiple baselines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablation studies, supplementary results, and both qualitative and quantitative metrics
Clear presentation with well-designed figures explaining the two-stage pipeline and Micro-Macro decomposition
Good reproducibility with promised code release and detailed hyperparameters in appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Micro-Macro decomposition is straightforward feature splitting; approach primarily combines existing techniques (IG-AE from Schnepf et al. 2024, Tri-Planes, latent NeRFs) without significant innovation
Narrow evaluation scope: only two synthetic/simple datasets (ShapeNet, Basel Faces) tested with very low 128×128 resolution; no complex real-world scenes or distribution shift analysis
Significant Stage 1 overhead (31.2 hours for 500 scenes) inadequately analyzed; break-even analysis missing, making it unclear when the method provides practical benefit

Incomplete quality analysis: claims 'comparable' rendering quality but shows mixed results (Basel slight improvement, ShapeNet slight degradation on perceptual metrics); no failure case analysis or advanced perceptual studies
Design choices lack justification: M=50 base planes, F_mic=10/F_mac=22 ratio appear arbitrary; ablation showing Ours-M=1 only modest drop questions necessity of multiple shared planes

Limited baseline comparisons: focuses on independent Tri-Planes but missing comparisons to transfer learning, meta-learning, or alternative scaling strategies; generalization to non-Tri-Plane representations unexplored

strengths: Clear identification of computational bottleneck in NeRF dataset generation with practical relevance
Comprehensive experimental details including detailed hyperparameters, algorithm description, and reproducible setup
Significant efficiency improvements demonstrated in Stage 2 (86% training time reduction, 68% memory reduction per scene)
Thorough ablation study (Table 3) validating each component contribution
Well-motivated Micro-Macro decomposition for capturing shared structure across similar scenes
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (latent NeRFs, Tri-Planes, shared representations) without significant novel insights or methodological advances
Problematic problem framing: 'scaled inverse graphics' is presented as novel, but training multiple NeRFs with shared structure is a straightforward application rather than a new problem

Unfair and incomplete comparisons: compares against methods (Instant-NGP, K-Planes, TensoRF) trained independently per-scene, not against methods designed for multi-scene learning; lacks comparison with other latent NeRF variants
Understated quality trade-offs: shows measurable degradation (SSIM 0.9498 vs 0.9512 on ShapeNet Cars; LPIPS higher) but claims 'comparable' quality without honest analysis
Substantial Stage 1 overhead inadequately addressed: requires 31.2 hours and 361 MB for just 500 scenes, limiting practical applicability for smaller datasets

Severely limited experimental scope: only two simple synthetic object datasets (ShapeNet Cars, Basel Faces) from constrained distributions; no complex scenes, unbounded environments, or real-world data
Questionable generalization properties: no evaluation of how quality degrades when Stage 2 scenes differ from Stage 1; assumes macro planes learned on 500 scenes generalize without validation
Missing critical analysis: no visualization of learned macro planes, no ablation on VAE choice, no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (N₁, M), no study of out-of-distribution generalization
Rendering efficiency claims partially misleading: 9.71 ms decoding time is substantial, reducing total rendering improvement from 98% to 56% when accounting for decoder overhead
Evaluation scope too limited: quality metrics computed on only 50 randomly sampled scenes due to baseline computational constraints, insufficient for confident claims

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical scalability challenges in NeRF-based 3D scene learning, relevant for 3D generative models and industrial applications
Solid technical approach combining latent space rendering with a novel Micro-Macro Tri-Plane decomposition that effectively shares information across scenes
Comprehensive experimental validation including detailed ablation studies (Table 3), precise resource cost measurements, and comparisons with recent methods (Instant-NGP, K-Planes, TensoRF)
Significant resource efficiency gains: ~86% reduction in per-scene training time and ~68% reduction in memory footprint for Stage 2 scenes, with favorable scalability demonstrated in Figure 5
Excellent reproducibility: complete algorithms, hyperparameter details, and promised code release enable easy reproduction and extension
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and logical flow from problem motivation through method to comprehensive experiments
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is combining existing techniques (Schnepf et al. 2024's latent space training, Tri-Planes) with a relatively simple Micro-Macro decomposition (feature concatenation + weighted summation); ablation shows most speedup comes from latent space rather than the decomposition

Significant Stage 1 overhead (31.2 hours, 361 MB for 500 scenes) limits practical applicability and accessibility of efficiency gains; no guidance on choosing N₁ or analysis of its impact on Stage 2 performance

Narrow evaluation scope: only 2 relatively simple datasets (synthetic ShapeNet Cars and front-facing Basel Faces); no evaluation on diverse real-world scenes, high-resolution imaging, or complex scene distributions
Rendering quality slightly inferior to baseline Tri-Planes (SSIM: 0.9498 vs 0.9512; LPIPS: 0.0367 vs 0.0346), which may limit applicability when quality is paramount

Insufficient ablation and sensitivity analysis: hyperparameter choices (M=50 base planes, F_mic=10, F_mac=22) appear arbitrary with limited justification; no systematic study of N₁ size or M value impact
Missing comparisons with alternative multi-scene or meta-learning approaches; comparison in Figure 1 uses independent training of baselines, which may not fairly represent potential competing methods

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: addresses genuine computational bottleneck in learning large sets of 3D scenes for generative modeling and reconstruction

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple datasets (ShapeNet, Basel Faces), extensive baselines (single-scene and many-scene methods), quantitative metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), and detailed resource cost analysis
Strong efficiency improvements: 7.2× training speedup and comparable/better memory usage versus Tri-Planes (8.96 min vs 64.32 min; 0.48 MB vs 1.50 MB per scene)
Clear methodology: intuitive micro-macro decomposition with scene-specific and shared components; well-explained two-stage training strategy
Thorough ablation studies: Table 2 justifies design choices (latent space, micro planes, macro planes, number of base planes)
Good scaling properties: efficiency gains increase with scene count, demonstrating value at intended scale
Reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters (Tables 13-14), Algorithm 1 pseudocode, promised open-source code
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines established techniques (micro-macro decomposition, shared representations, latent NeRFs) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Critical reliance on unpublished concurrent work: the '3D-aware latent space' from Anonymous (2025) is unavailable and unverifiable; significant performance gains may originate from this component rather than Fused-Planes, making novelty attribution unclear and reproducibility compromised

Confounded ablation studies: Table 2 conflates latent space and micro-macro contributions; no ablation comparing two-stage vs. single-pass training or assessing true contribution of Fused-Planes architecture without concurrent Anonymous work
Evaluation limited to synthetic data: only ShapeNet and Basel Faces (simple objects and faces); no real-world 3D data; unclear scalability to complex large-scale scenes or heterogeneous datasets
Limited evaluation robustness: only 16 ShapeNet and 4 Basel scenes assessed (acknowledged computational limitation) reduces result robustness and sensitivity to scene selection

Rendering quality trade-offs underexplored: Fused-Planes PSNR (30.47) lower than K-Planes (30.88), TensoRF (36.74), SPARF-128 (31.07); paper claims 'maintaining similar quality' but lacks nuanced analysis; no Pareto frontier discussion
Arbitrary design choices without justification: N₁=500/N₂=1500 split lacks ablation; M=50 base planes unjustified; no sensitivity analysis for critical hyperparameters
Missing learned representation analysis: no visualization of base planes; no interpretation of what shared components capture; no analysis of weight distributions or transferability across datasets

Experimental design issues: CodeNeRF (MSIG) is author-proposed adaptation with unclear optimality; different N₁ values for compared methods (CodeNeRF: N₁=1000 vs Fused-Planes: N₁=500) complicates direct comparison; comparison includes method (SPARF) with known texture failure modes

Incomplete technical details: weight normalization and constraints not explicitly specified; no exploration of joint training as alternative to two-stage; inherits biases from pretrained Stable Diffusion VAE

Presentation issues: reference to 'Anonymous (2025)' breaks anonymity and creates confusion; Figure 1 cluttered; critical details relegated to appendices; unclear contribution attribution between latent space and Fused-Planes

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem of efficiently learning large sets of 3D scenes
Comprehensive experimental breadth with multiple datasets, metrics, and baseline types
Good reproducibility provisions with detailed hyperparameters and promised open-source code
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of efficiency-quality tradeoffs
Thoughtful ablation study showing contribution of individual components (latent space, micro/macro planes)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (micro-macro decomposition, latent NeRF, two-stage training) rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts
Critical unresolved dependency on Anonymous (2025) for the 3D-aware latent space, making it difficult to assess what contribution is novel to this work vs. borrowed from that paper
Modest empirical improvements over Tri-Planes baseline (2.3 PSNR on ShapeNet, 0.8 on Basel Faces) and no improvement over state-of-the-art (SPARF-128 achieves better quality)
Evaluation limited to only 4 scenes per category, all synthetic data (ShapeNet, Basel Faces), raising concerns about result generalizability and significance
Unfair baseline comparisons: CodeNeRF (MSIG) evaluated with different split (N₁=1000) than Fused-Planes (N₁=500); CodeNeRF variant adapted by authors themselves

Insufficient ablation on critical hyperparameters: number of base planes M only tested at M=1 in ablations despite significant impact (27.69 vs 28.64 PSNR); no guidance on choosing M or sensitivity analysis

Lack of analysis on what the method actually learns: no visualization of learned base planes, no investigation of whether micro-macro decomposition meaningfully separates scene-specific vs. common features
Memory advantage primarily comes from VAE component (m₀=360.75 MB), limiting practical scaling benefit for smaller MSIG problems (Figure 5 shows advantage minimal for N<100)
Complex two-stage training procedure with multiple loss functions and hyperparameters appears ad-hoc with limited justification for design choices
All datasets are object-centric or simple; no evaluation on realistic large-scale scenes or diverse real-world data

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear practical applications in 3D reconstruction and generative modeling
Clean architectural design with intuitive micro-macro decomposition enabling parameter sharing while maintaining expressivity
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple datasets, extensive baseline comparisons, multiple quality metrics, and thorough ablation studies
Strong empirical efficiency results: 7.16-8.96 min per-scene training with 0.48 MB memory while maintaining competitive PSNR (30.47 vs. 28.15 for Tri-Planes) and demonstrating good scaling properties
Excellent reproducibility: promised open-source code, detailed hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, and comprehensive supplementary material
Fair experimental methodology including CodeNeRF (MSIG) baseline adaptation for fair comparison and consistent evaluation conditions across methods
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily an engineering combination of existing techniques (Tri-Planes + micro-macro sharing + latent space training); micro-macro decomposition is similar to conditional NeRFs in CodeNeRF
Critical dependency on concurrent unpublished work (Anonymous 2025) for 3D-aware latent space, obscuring the contribution boundary and making it difficult to assess independent novelty
Evaluation restricted to synthetic data only (ShapeNet objects and synthetic Basel Faces); no real-world scenes or realistic image conditions; generalization properties remain unvalidated

Quality-efficiency tradeoff incompletely analyzed: SPARF-128 achieves PSNR 31.07 vs. Fused-Planes 30.47; significant gap remains vs. single-scene methods (e.g., TensoRF 36.74); claims about maintaining Tri-Planes quality not uniformly supported across metrics

Insufficient design justification: no ablation studies for M (only M=1 tested), feature dimensions (F_mic, F_mac), or subset split ratio (N1=500, N2=1500); warm-up procedure lacks principled justification
Small evaluation sample size (4 test scenes per dataset) due to computational constraints; per-scene results show high variance, limiting conclusion robustness
Missing interpretability analysis: no visualization of learned base planes vs. micro planes; no analysis of distribution shift between subsets or robustness to initialization

Restricted applicability scope: only many-view NVS setting; latent space requirement may limit applications requiring RGB-space representations; cannot evaluate in few-view regime where multi-scene approach most beneficial
Incomplete technical justification for two-stage training design choices (e.g., why freeze encoder in subset 2?); unclear generalization when subset 2 has different distribution from subset 1
Rendering efficiency gains (2.3× vs. Tri-Planes) mentioned but not systematically compared with all baselines; inference time analysis limited
